newsitem.title: USA: Lawyer says U.S. soldier was too drunk to murder.
newsitem.headline: Lawyer says U.S. soldier was too drunk to murder.

text.p: Defence lawyers for James Burmeister launched their case Monday by claiming the former paratrooper was so drunk he should have been in a blackout when two people were murdered.
Fayetteville adjoins the Fort Bragg military installation, home to the 82nd Airborne Division, and Burmeister, 21, and two fellow soldiers were drinking in a bar there before the murders.
Burmeister is charged with first-degree murder in the deaths of Jackie Burden, 27, and Michael James, 36, shot at close range as they walked in a Fayetteville neighbourhood on Dec. 7, 1995.
Lawyers attacked the prosecution's theory that he killed the couple because they were black and to raise his status in a racist skinhead group.
Pharmacology professor Brian McMillen told the jury that Burmeister was too drunk to have killed anyone intentionally.
"Burmeister's ability to plan the murders was severely impaired," said McMillen, who teaches at the School of Medicine at East Carolina University in Greenville, North Carolina.

Using charts and graphs, he told the jury Burmeister's blood alcohol level was .259 at the height of his drinking spree -- more than triple the limit considered legally drunk in North Carolina. He said alcohol levels of .25 or higher cause "alchoholic blackout."
Over the past two weeks, jurors heard Burmeister, of Thompson, Pennsylvania, characterised as "pure, unmitigated evil" by prosecutors, who plan to seek the death penalty.
His friend, Randy Meadows, who was accused of driving Burmeister and Malcolm Wright, another white ex-soldier, to the area where the killings occurred, confessed and turned state's witness.

Meadows told police he heard six gunshots after Burmeister and Wright got out of the car. He also said Burmeister wanted to earn a "spider web" tattoo, a skinhead symbol police say represents the killing of a homosexual or a black person.
Police later found white supremacist and bomb-making literature and a Nazi flag at Burmeister's trailer home.
Meadows testified Burmeister admitted killing the black couple and joked he was jailed for "performing a community service."
Wright, 22, of Lexington, Kentucky, will be tried in March on charges of murder and conspiracy to commit murder. He also faces the death penalty.
